neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, interactive, anxious. Normal age-appropriate behavior.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. Extraocular movements intact. Pupils equal and reactive. No facial weakness. Normal head control.
neurological_exam.motor: Refuses to stand or bear weight. In prone position, left lower extremity moves less than right. In supine, can lift right thigh slightly but not left when stimulated. Both hands: markedly weak grip strength. Cannot rise from floor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Difficult to assess in 2-year-old. No obvious sensory level. No withdrawal from painful stimuli appears intact.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Complete global areflexia — absent bilaterally in all extremities. No knee jerks, ankle jerks, or biceps reflexes.
neurological_exam.coordination: Cannot formally assess. Balance markedly impaired when attempting to stand.
neurological_exam.gait: Refuses to walk. Last walked normally 24 hours prior.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: Unable to perform formal FVC in 2-year-old — clinical respiratory assessment: tidal breathing appears adequate, crying is vigorous, SpO2 100% on room air. Pneumonia treated with cefdinir 3 weeks ago (now resolved). Varicella, hepatitis A, and influenza vaccines received 4 days ago. Last bowel movement 36 hours ago (baseline: daily). No fever at presentation. No trauma. No history of developmental delay.

patient.chief_complaint: Twenty-four-hour history of refusing to walk in a toddler with normal development — left-predominant leg weakness and global areflexia, preceded by pneumonia and vaccines 4 days prior.
patient.history_present_illness: A 2-year-old girl is brought by her father because she will not walk. Twenty-four hours ago she was walking normally at baseline. Over the past 24 hours, weakness has progressed to difficulty crawling, with greater weakness on the left side. Three weeks ago she had pneumonia successfully treated with a 10-day course of cefdinir. Four days ago she received varicella, hepatitis A, and influenza vaccines at her well-child visit. She has no fever at presentation. She has not had a bowel movement in 36 hours, compared to her daily baseline. She has no history of developmental delay or prior neurological symptoms. Her maternal grandmother has multiple sclerosis, but there is no family history of hereditary neuropathy. There is no history of trauma, toxic ingestion, or insect bites. On examination, she is alert and interactive but will not bear weight. Her left leg moves noticeably less than the right. Her hand grip is markedly weak bilaterally. Global areflexia is present on detailed examination — this is the critical finding that distinguishes GBS from functional or musculoskeletal causes of refusal to walk. The combination of acute onset of weakness in a normally developing toddler, global areflexia, and antecedent respiratory illness followed by vaccines places GBS (AIDP) high on the differential. The pediatric GBS workup focuses on excluding cord compression, toxic exposure, metabolic causes, and infection before confirming GBS with CSF analysis.

quantitative_data.pattern: Demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy meeting GBS criteria — using pediatric age-corrected reference values

specialized_test.impression: NCS/EMG confirms AIDP in this 2-year-old: markedly prolonged DMLs (using age-corrected values), reduced CVs, absent F-waves and H-reflex bilaterally, reduced sural SNAPs. Pattern meets Brighton Collaboration Level 1 GBS criteria. Pediatric AIDP diagnosis confirmed.

Respiratory surveillance — formal FVC not measurable in toddler; monitor clinical signs of respiratory distress

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, pediatric AIDP (post-respiratory illness and post-vaccine), seronegative

differential.key_features: No tick found on thorough head/skin examination; tick removal would cause rapid resolution
No honey exposure; descending not ascending pattern; autonomic features; no toxin exposure
No cord lesion on MRI; areflexia not UMN signs; no sensory level
Immunized; polio is asymmetric and motor only; no fever preceding paralysis

optimal_actions.action: CT head — exclude intracranial pathology in altered/declining child
Thorough skin exam for ticks — tick paralysis is a GBS mimic in children

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Protein 25 mg/dL (elevated for pediatric) with 2 WBCs

optimal_actions.action: Pediatric ICU admission — respiratory monitoring via SpO2 and clinical assessment (FVC not feasible)

critical_actions: Tick paralysis must be excluded with full skin/scalp examination before GBS diagnosis — tick paralysis mimics GBS exactly and is treated by tick removal
IVIG pediatric dosing: 2 g/kg total (given as 1 g/kg/day x 2 days OR 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) — same mechanism as adult but weight-based
Formal FVC is not possible in toddlers — clinical respiratory assessment replaces: monitor cry strength, accessory muscle use, SpO2
Pediatric CSF protein norms are lower — protein 25 mg/dL is elevated for a 2-year-old (upper normal ~20 mg/dL)
Maternal history of MS does not indicate hereditary neuropathy — no increased genetic risk for GBS from MS family history
contraindicated_actions: Succinylcholine if intubation required — use rocuronium
Discharging without ICU admission — pediatric GBS can deteriorate rapidly
key_reasoning_points: Pediatric GBS: refusal to walk in a previously walking toddler with global areflexia is a GBS presentation — the child cannot articulate weakness but the clinical exam reveals it
Tick paralysis is the most important GBS mimic in children — remove the tick and symptoms reverse rapidly; thorough scalp and skin examination is mandatory
Post-vaccine GBS: vaccines are a recognized GBS trigger in rare cases; the temporal relationship (4 days post-vaccine) is clinically relevant
Concurrent pneumonia 3 weeks prior is likely the primary GBS trigger — respiratory infections (Mycoplasma, influenza) are common pediatric GBS triggers
NCS reference values in children are age-corrected — lower CVs are normal in toddlers; values must be compared to pediatric norms

red_herrings.data_point: Varicella, hepatitis A, influenza vaccines received 4 days ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute GBS to vaccine reaction and delay systemic workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: While vaccines are a rare GBS trigger, the pneumonia 3 weeks prior is a more likely trigger; vaccine-associated GBS is managed identically to other GBS — IVIG regardless of cause

metadata.difficulty_description: Pediatric GBS in 2-year-old toddler — refusal to walk; tick paralysis must be excluded; FVC not feasible; pediatric CSF protein norms lower
